sources.title: OpenStax Calculus Volume 1: Defining the Derivative
sources.author: OpenStax
sources.content: A secant line through two points gives an average rate of change. As the second point approaches the first, the limiting secant slope defines the tangent-line slope when the limit exists. The derivative at a point is the limit of the difference quotient. For f(x)=x squared, simplifying the difference quotient before taking the limit produces f prime of a equal to 2a.

sources.title: OpenStax Calculus Volume 1: The Derivative as a Function
sources.author: OpenStax
sources.content: The derivative function assigns a derivative value to each input where the defining limit exists. Positive derivative values correspond to positive tangent slopes, negative values to negative slopes, and zero to horizontal tangents. Differentiability at a point implies continuity. Discontinuities, corners or cusps, and vertical tangents are standard ways differentiability can fail.

sources.title: OpenStax Calculus Volume 1: Derivatives as Rates of Change
sources.author: OpenStax
sources.content: The derivative represents an instantaneous rate of change. For motion along a line, the derivative of position is velocity and the derivative of velocity is acceleration. Rates have units formed from output units divided by input units. Applications also include population growth and marginal quantities.

sources.title: OpenStax Calculus Volume 1: Linear Approximations and Differentials
sources.author: OpenStax
sources.content: At a differentiable point a, the linearization L(x)=f(a)+f prime(a)(x-a) uses the tangent line to approximate f(x) for x near a. Equivalently, a small change in output can be approximated by f prime(a) times a small change in input. The approximation is local and its error depends on the function and distance from the base point.
